title: Mapping the Moon with a laser
purpose: Teach how LOLA measures height with laser echoes, how heights become a map and slopes, and how a safe road is planned from them.

beats.label: measured
beats.credit: NASA LRO LOLA · GSFC PGDA · the Aurora ridge, {mpp} m per point, shaded for clarity
beats.here: The real ridge where Aurora stands

beats.label: model
beats.credit: Numbers computed from LOLA heights · drawing not to scale

captions: NASA's LRO spacecraft fires laser pulses at the Moon from orbit.
Timing each echo gives the distance, and so the height of the ground.
Millions of those heights make a map, down to one point every {mpp} m.
This is the real ridge where Aurora stands.
Two NASA maps of it agree to about {rms} m.
From heights you get slopes: how steep each step is.
So the road to the cold trap is {road_len} km, never steeper than {road_slope}°.
ends_on: Real maps make real plans. Check the slope on the map before you drive.
